narrative.overview:
Every surface is set like a page of an open pocket dictionary. A running head carries guide words (the first and last headword of today's queue) over a single red rule; the deck list below is ranked the way a dictionary ranks entries, by weight and indent, separated by hairlines; thumb-cut tabs hang off the page's fore-edge, one per top-level deck branch. The card itself, when the plugin draws it, is a dictionary entry: headword, red reading, italic part of speech, meaning, then a ruled-off example.

The system owns almost no colour of its own. Ground, ink, font and every neutral come from the active Obsidian theme, so the page follows any theme in light and dark. On top of that sits one dictionary red and a small set of muted pigments, each with a fixed meaning. Density is calm: one body size, generous vertical air around the due figure, a single large number as the only display type in the chrome.

The build rejects the dashboard of equal stat cards and coloured count tables; numbers are set as text in columns, and history is a quiet footnote in ink density.
keyCharacteristics: Theme ground and ink; one dictionary red; muted pigments with fixed meanings.
A 2px red rule under every head (running head, browser toolbar, code block head, finished title, entry head).
Hairline rules instead of boxes; rows ranked by weight and indent.
Thumb-cut tabs on the page's fore-edge, in a six-pigment sequence.
Tabular numerals everywhere a count appears; zeros fade.

rules.name: The One Red Rule
rules.body: Red means "due today" or "this is the head". It never decorates; it marks the head rule, due counts and the one primary action.

rules.name: The Fixed Pigment Rule
rules.body: New is green, learning is ochre, due is red, and the grades read red, ochre, green, blue from Again to Easy. A pigment never changes meaning between screens.

rules.name: The Thumb Sequence Rule
rules.body: Thumb tabs take pigments in order: red, ochre, olive, green, blue, violet, then repeat. Tabs are tinted at 16% over paper at rest and filled when active.

rules.name: The Ink Density Rule
rules.body: History is shown in ink, not hue: the review heatmap steps the theme's text colour through 18%, 32%, 50% and 70%. The forecast bars are the one exception, red at 55% because they are future due counts.

rules.name: The Theme Owns the Ground Rule
rules.body: Every neutral is an Obsidian variable or a mix of one. No hard-coded greys or backgrounds in the chrome.

rules.name: The One Body Size Rule
rules.body: Rank comes from weight, indent and ink level, not a stack of type sizes. Deck depth 0 is semibold, depth 1 normal, depths 2 and 3 muted.

rules.name: The Tabular Count Rule
rules.body: Every count is set in tabular numerals in a fixed right-aligned column, so figures line up down the page.

rules.name: The Rule-Not-Box Rule
rules.body: Structure is drawn with hairlines (row dividers, the list's top rule, the fore-edge) and the 2px red head rule. Containers do not get borders and shadows to separate them.

dos: Do take every neutral from Obsidian variables (`--background-primary`, `--text-normal`, `--text-muted`, `--text-faint`) or a `color-mix` of them, and check both light and dark themes.
Do put a 2px red rule under each head, and keep hairlines (12% and 22% ink) for every other division.
Do keep the pigment meanings fixed: green new, ochre learning, red due; Again red, Hard ochre, Good green, Easy blue.
Do fade zero counts to faint ink at normal weight.
Do set counts in tabular numerals in fixed right-aligned columns.
Do use the deep red fill for filled buttons with white text, and the lighter red for text and rules.
donts: Don't build equal stat cards or coloured count tables; counts are text in columns.
Don't use red for decoration or for anything that is not a head rule, a due count, the primary action, focus or selection.
Don't add hue to history; review activity is ink density.
Don't bundle web fonts or hard-code greys and backgrounds in the chrome.
Don't box containers with borders and shadows; separate with rules and tonal steps.
